But how else would you put it ? Since Gord Johnston took over as CEO at the beginning of 2018 , Stantec 's market cap has risen from roughly $4 billion to nearly $18 billion . The company took about six decades to build its annual net @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , that number has almost doubled , to about $6 billion in 2024 , while its adjusted EBITDA has nearly tripled , to $980 million . " <p> There are a lot of reasons for the recent success , but they boil down to two : the moment Stantec finds itself in and the man at the top . And it 's no secret to anyone familiar with the company 's rise that , for a while , it looked like it might go a whole other way . <p> Gord Johnston has set a goal for the company : to be the world 's top integrated engineering , architecture and environment services firm . <p> We 've entered a golden age of engineering and design . <p> In the United States , the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act alone is pushing over US$1.2 trillion of government funding into water , transportation , broadband and power-grid projects . It 's the deal that nearly derailed the company . And it 's Stantec 's recovery from that debacle that forms the foundational story @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a firm , it becomes Stantec forever . And so the cultural piece is so important . " <p> -- Gord Johnston , CEO of Stantec <p> In the 71-year history of Stantec , there have been just five CEOs , starting with the founder , Don " Doc " Stanley , who passed up a chance to play for the Boston Bruins to start a one-man engineering firm in Edmonton . After almost 30 years of building the business , he handed the reins to Ron Triffo , who diversified it and took it public , a $30-million firm in 1994 . Then it was Tony Franceschini , who set his sights on growth , pushing the company from 1,200 people to more than 10,000 . Fourth came Bob Gomes , who got Stantec through the aftermath of the financial crisis and then , in 2015 , with growth prospects in North America dimming , thought it was time to take a big leap . <p> Based in Colorado , MWH Global specialized in water infrastructure and natural resources . With 187 offices in 26 countries , and a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Stantec immediate global reach , while its 6,800 employees would boost the company 's workforce by almost half . <p> On top of that , a major part of MWH 's business was construction , a vertical Stantec had never been able to offer . Alone , the construction segment would contribute about 15% of Stantec 's future revenue . <p> " We thought that aspect of it would be complementary , " says board chair Doug Ammerman , who as a director at the time supported Gomes 's decision . They announced the deal in March of 2016 . <p> Things went sideways quickly . It turned out that construction revenue was lumpy . Much of the money for a project came up front , then nothing for months . Estimating costs was hard , and delays dragged on the bottom line . One of the beauties of the engineering and consulting business model -- wherein the company designs a project and then oversees construction carried out by someone else -- is that delays actually generate revenue . That bridge is going to take six months longer than you @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ billable hours ; the costs are someone else 's problem . <p> Amid the new uncertainty , Stantec started missing earnings targets . Margins fell . Its stock bumped along for a year while its relationship with the investment community deteriorated . Problems with the construction segment became the focus of quarterly calls with analysts . Some within the company began to treat the relationship with investors as hostile and adversarial . <p> In mid-2017 , Stantec announced that it was searching for a new CEO . Says the chair , " It was n't automatic that person was going to be Gord . " <p> Johnston had had an on-and-off relationship with Stantec . Schooled in engineering , he started in the ' 90s after working for the City of Edmonton and then the Province of Alberta . Water was his specialty -- designing upgrades to wastewater treatment plants and the like . Not long after joining Stantec , he realized that he liked people more than his calculator and started working more with clients . Soon the company was sending him places , first to an office in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to help run a project in Kuwait . <p> There in the desert , he saw first-hand the destructiveness of poor middle management . A supervisor in Kuwait was n't , in Johnston 's opinion , living up to Stantec 's values of collaboration and mutual support . " I thought my boss was a jerk , " he says . So he quit . Went to work for a competitor in an office in Mississauga . <p> Eventually , though , he and his wife felt the need to rejoin their families in Alberta . So he hooked up with Stantec again and rose quickly . In 2012 , he was senior VP , water . Three years later , executive VP , infrastructure . That was the job he held when then board chair , Aram Keith , asked if he 'd like to be considered for CEO . <p> A big part of his pitch to the board boiled down to : Sell construction . This has created a great deal of uncertainty for both Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities . When multiple First Nations assert overlapping or conflicting claims to large areas , it leaves many British Columbians confused about how these issues will be resolved and what the implications will be for public land . <p> There is no question that some Indigenous communities in B.C. had land wrongfully taken from them , including documented cases in the South Okanagan . @@131800521 <h> On both sides of the political divide , people value accurate beliefs . <h> Key points <p> When people adopt false political beliefs , this may stem from a lack of access to the best information . <p> People share a desire to know the truth , so common ground should be achievable with patience and humility . <p> Source : Annie Spratt / Unsplash <p> Thanksgiving is a time of plentiful food and bitter political disputes . Studies have suggested that attempts to avoid talking about politics have significantly shortened the time that families spend together during Thanksgiving . If you , like many other Americans , are dreading a Thanksgiving meal spent trying to reason with relatives who refuse to listen to reason , what are you to do ? Rather than disengaging , I suggest leaning into discussions about the evidence underlying your political beliefs . <p> As a cognitive scientist studying how people form ideological attitudes , I have been impressed by research showing that we can shed some of the common pessimism about political disagreements . Studies repeatedly show that our deeply held beliefs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and that we do not gullibly accept partisan claims . Beliefs in falsehoods likely stem from earnest efforts to seek accuracy within insulated echo chambers ( for example , by only consuming news supporting one 's views ) , rather than from partisans purposely hiding their heads in the sand . If people generally pursue the truth but lack access to the best available information , this opens up greater potential for productive Thanksgiving conversations . <p> One likely influence on the pursuit of accurate beliefs is whether or not truth-seeking is thought to be good . Yet , there is surprisingly little known about how people judge others who strive to form true beliefs in partisan situations where beliefs are strong markers of group membership , and whether these evaluations change as we develop from children into adults . Do people prefer others who seek objective knowledge or others who display loyalty to ideological dogma ? I recently set out to illuminate this question along with 10 colleagues . Our research findings have just been published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology : General . <p> In our first @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ adults with scenarios about Republicans or Democrats encountering members of the opposing party who disagreed with them about a polarized issue like gun control or privatizing prisons . The protagonist in each scenario then consulted a nonpartisan website , ProCon.org , where they were surprised to discover that the available evidence favored their opponent 's belief . We asked our participants whether it was good or bad for the protagonist to have sought out additional information , to change their mind upon encountering this evidence , and to tell co-partisans that the opposing political party 's belief was correct . All three tendencies were rated quite positively , though this was especially true when people were evaluating protagonists who belonged to their political outgroups ( and thus were considering the beliefs of participants ' ingroups ) . <p> An example image from the fictional scenarios in Study 2 . <p> Source : Allysa Adams and Valerie Zizik / Used with permission <p> In our second study , we presented 6- to 9-year-old children and adults with fictional scenarios to reduce the impact of preexisting beliefs . In one scenario , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an historic race ; in another , the groups disagreed about which animal species was permissible to take scales from in order to manufacture a lifesaving medicine . Once again , we found overwhelming evidence that information-seeking , belief change , and truth-sharing were considered praiseworthy . This pattern held true across age groups . <p> Overall , our research shows that people believe the pursuit of accuracy is more praiseworthy than the pursuit of partisanship . <p> This central finding is consequential . As policymakers and others attempt to combat unfounded beliefs , it is critical for them to know that people do not endorse forming beliefs on partisan grounds . Rather than trying to improve faulty reasoning , success is instead likely to stem from improving access to reliable sources of information . <p> These results also give us reason to spend more time talking about politics with relatives who favor the other side of the political aisle . If we all share a desire to know the truth , then common ground should be achievable . But this will take patience , care , and humility . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there will often be many layers of beliefs that will require re-evaluation . For instance , a Democrat who merely points to a few scientific publications showing the dangers of climate change or the benefits of vaccination will do little to change the minds of their Republican relatives . Succeeding on this front will require finding out whether these relatives think they have stronger evidence supporting their stances , whether they have good reasons to mistrust the objectivity of scientists , and whether certain values are contributing to their attitudes in ways that are overriding factual beliefs . It will also require non-combativeness , such that discussions can feel collaborative rather than defensive . A shared focus on discerning the truth should help with this .

@@131834373 <h> ECCC launches new colour-coded Canadian weather alerts <p> Environment and Climate Change Canada will use a three-colour system to convey the risk posed by weather hazards across the country <p> You 'll soon notice a colourful change to the weather alerts issued for your area by Environment and Climate Change Canada ( ECCC ) . <p> Beginning Nov. 26 , 2025 , the agency will unveil colour-coded alerts across the country . <p> This new system will help Canadians understand and prepare for the level of weather impacts possible during hazardous conditions . <h> Understanding the alert colours <p> Every weather watch , advisory , and warning issued by ECCC will now have a colour attached to convey the potential risk posed by each hazard . <p> Yellow alerts indicate that hazardous weather may cause " damage , disruption , or health impacts " in your area . Yellow is the most common type of alert , advising that impacts are expected to be moderate and localized . <p> Orange alerts are less common , signalling the risk for severe weather that may cause significant damage , disruption , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ orange alert may lead to major and widespread impacts , potentially lasting for up to a few days . <p> Content continues below <p> Red alerts are rare and reserved for the most urgent situations , when very dangerous and possibly life-threatening weather may cause extreme damage and disruption . Communities under a red weather alert could expect extensive , widespread , and prolonged impacts . <p> For example , you 'll now see alerts displayed in the following format : <p> Yellow Advisory - Fog <p> Orange Watch - Severe Thunderstorm <p> Red Warning - Rain <h> Colours chosen based on impacts and confidence <p> Meteorologists with ECCC will choose a colour to convey a weather alert 's risk level based on both forecast confidence and possible weather impacts . <p> Some factors that determine a weather event 's potential impacts include property damage , travel delays , power outages , health dangers , and how long it may take for the affected areas to recover afterward . <p> Greater confidence and greater impacts will necessitate a higher risk level . For instance , high confidence in a high-impact @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are only issued when forecasters are very confident in extreme severe weather impacts . <h> Historical examples of the new alert system in action <p> Here are some examples of how these new alerts will work in everyday practice . <p> Content continues below <p> A chinook wind event in southern Alberta produced localized gusts capable of scattered tree damage and short-term power outages . Given the moderate impacts expected , forecasters would likely have issued a Yellow Warning - Wind for this event . <p> Widespread freezing rain affected southern Ontario in March 2025 . Some communities saw more than 20 mm of ice accretion , and around one million homes and businesses lost power . ECCC would have issued an Orange Warning - Ice for this event . <p> An unprecedented atmospheric river event swept into southern British Columbia in November 2021 , causing an estimated $450 million in damages . This is the type of high-end event for which forecasters reserve red alerts . The historic deluge would have received a Red Warning - Rain from ECCC forecasters.

@@131873543 <p> Groundbreaking new research warns that Africa 's forests , once vital allies in the fight against climate change , have turned from a carbon sink into a carbon source . <p> A new international study published in Scientific Reports and led by researchers at the National Centre for Earth Observation at the Universities of Leicester , Sheffield and Edinburgh reveals that Africa 's forests , which have long absorbed carbon dioxide from the atmosphere , are now releasing more carbon than they remove . <p> This alarming shift , which happened after 2010 , underscores the urgent need for stronger global action to protect forests , a major focus of the COP30 Climate Summit that concluded last week in Brazil . <p> Using advanced satellite data and machine learning , the researchers tracked more than a decade of changes in aboveground forest biomass , the amount of carbon stored in trees and woody vegetation . They found that while Africa gained carbon between 2007 and 2010 , widespread forest loss in tropical rainforests has since tipped the balance . <p> Between 2010 and 2017 , the continent lost approximately @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is equivalent to the weight of about 106 million cars . Gains in savanna regions due to shrub growth have not been enough to offset the losses . <p> Professor Heiko Balzter , senior author and Director of the Institute for Environmental Futures at the University of Leicester , said : " This is a critical wake-up call for global climate policy . If Africa 's forests are no longer absorbing carbon , it means other regions and the world as a whole will need to cut greenhouse gas emissions even more deeply to stay within the 2 ? C goal of the Paris Agreement and avoid catastrophic climate change . Climate finance for the Tropical Forests Forever Facility must be scaled up quickly to put an end to global deforestation for good . " <p> The research draws on data from NASA 's spaceborne laser instrument called GEDI and Japan 's ALOS radar satellites , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It would pay forested countries to leave their tropical forests untouched . The results show that without urgent action to stop forest loss , the world risks losing one of its most important natural carbon buffers . <p> Dr Nezha Acil , co-author from the National Centre for Earth Observation at the University of Leicester 's Institute for Environmental Futures , said : " Stronger forest governance , enforcement against illegal logging , and large-scale restoration programs such as AFR100 , which aims to restore 100 million hectares of African landscapes by 2030 , can make a huge difference in reversing the damage done . @@131874214 <h> Canada introduces new colour-coded weather alert system <p> Weather alerts issued by Environment and Climate Change Canada will now be accompanied by a colour indicating possible severity and confidence in the prediction . <p> Alerts will now come with a yellow , orange or red label to indicate the seriousness of an event . <p> The change is being made to make weather information and risk easier to understand at a glance , ECCC said this week , and to align with international best practices . <p> Yellow alerts will be issued when hazardous weather is forecast that could cause moderate or short-term damage or health impacts . <p> Orange alerts will be issued when severe weather is likely to cause significant damage or health impacts and the effect could last a few days . <p> While red alerts will be rare , they will be issued when there is a high probability of very dangerous and possibly life-threatening weather and the impact is predicted to be extensive @@131906182 <p> Prime Minister Mark Carney is throwing his government 's support behind Alberta 's controversial new pipeline proposal in a deal that scraps , suspends and softens major federal climate policies for the oil-rich province , and puts in question the long-standing oil tanker ban off the north coast of British Columbia . <p> OTTAWA -- Prime Minister Mark Carney is throwing his government 's support behind Alberta 's controversial new pipeline proposal in a deal that scraps , suspends and softens major federal climate policies for the oil-rich province , and puts in question the long-standing oil tanker ban off the north coast of British Columbia . <p> Taken together , Thursday 's memorandum of understanding marks a significant shift in Ottawa 's approach to climate and energy politics , placing peace with Alberta over the national regulations favoured under Carney 's predecessor , Justin Trudeau . <p> It also spotlighted rifts inside the government , prompting Steven Guilbeault -- the prominent climate activist who helped craft many of those policies -- to resign from Carney 's cabinet on Thursday while decrying the deal and declare the Liberal government @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> After the memorandum , gone is the planned cap on emissions from the oil and gas sector . National clean electricity rules are suspended in Alberta alone until at least next April , possibly beyond -- and possibly for other province 's too , according to Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson . Alberta 's fossil-fuel industry will also get softer targets for reductions in emissions of methane , a potent greenhouse gas , than Ottawa planned for less than two years ago . <p> On its end , Alberta agreed to work with Ottawa to strengthen its provincial industrial carbon price . The accord also links the completion of its preferred pipeline proposal to the financing and construction of the massive proposed Pathways Alliance carbon capture development , with the accord describing each project as a " prerequisite " for the other . <p> Additionally , the federal government committed to , if necessary for a pipeline , lifting or changing Ottawa 's ban on large oil tanker traffic off northern B.C. 's coast -- a policy that B.C. and coastal First Nations have demanded must remain in effect @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sensitive area that includes the pristine Great Bear Rainforest . <p> The accord also referenced construction of " one or more " new private sector pipelines , on top of any additional expansion of the Trans Mountain pipeline system that already carries oil from Alberta to the B.C. coast . <p> In a speech marking the accord at the Calgary Chamber of Commerce , the prime minister received two standing ovations and framed the deal as part of the government 's wider plan to juice the economy and fast-track development projects as it grapples with the U.S. trade war . <p> " We used to explore in this country . " Anxieties also surfaced in Carney 's Liberal caucus on Parliament Hill , where some MPs were " hopping mad " about being left out of talks about the deal , and some questioned whether it would harm the party politically , sources told the Star . <p> Several environmental groups denounced the deal , with the Canadian Climate Institute declaring it risks " unravelling " the country 's contribution to the global fight against climate change . <p> In Calgary , a jubilant Alberta Premier Danielle Smith hailed the five-page memorandum as a road map to " removing and revising " environmental policies that her government has railed against for years . @@131908370 <h> Ronald Sanders Cost of less than a cup of coffee could end world hunger in five years <p> This commentary is dedicated to Patrick Cozier of Barbados , whose probing occasioned its writing . <p> In my article last week , ' Hunger and war : The oldest crime the world still permits ' , I argued that global hunger is not caused by a lack of food but by political decisions that produce war , destroy livelihoods , and block humanitarian access . That view is echoed by the United Nations ( UN ) : a recent briefing on food insecurity , drawing on World Food Programme ( WFP ) analysis , noted that ending hunger by 2030 would cost about US$93 billion a year , while governments have spent US$21.9 trillion on their militaries over the last decade . <p> Those figures from the UN and WFP show that US$93 billion per year -- less than one per cent of that military spending -- would end global hunger . The contrast exposes the chasm between our professed values and our actual priorities . <p> If the world @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fraction of that to feed the hungry . But outrage alone fills no stomach . We need action . That is why I am suggesting here a clear , affordable way to do so : a global humanitarian contribution of just US$0.75 for every barrel of oil produced , applied for five years . That task is not easy , but the arithmetic is simple . <p> Data based on the US Energy Information Administration show that global petroleum and liquids supply in 2023 averaged about 101.8 million barrels per day -- roughly 37 billion barrels a year . A contribution of US$0.75 per barrel , if applied to all globally produced barrels , would raise about US$28 billion annually -- around US$140 billion over five years -- nearly US$50 billion more than the UN 's estimate of what is needed to eradicate hunger . <h> Headlines Delivered to Your Inbox <h> END HUNGER <p> For every US$100 earned from selling a barrel of oil , just 75 cents would end hunger . Even at modest oil prices , such a levy amounts to well under one per cent of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ swings . Yet , for hundreds of millions of people , that 75 cents would mean survival . <p> The concentration of global oil production makes coordination feasible . Various international energy datasets show that a relatively small group of major producers -- including the United States , Saudi Arabia , Russia , Canada , China , Iraq , Brazil , the United Arab Emirates , Iran and Kuwait -- accounts for most of the world 's output . <p> From a geopolitical standpoint , the fact that so much production is centred in a small number of countries adds weight to the moral argument . Those who extract vast value from the earth have both the capacity and , arguably , the responsibility to contribute to humanity 's survival . <p> Oil and gas revenues have enriched producing states and their companies and helped fuel global development . But the same fossil-fuel use has driven climate change and intensified droughts , floods and storms that destroy crops , displace people , and deepen food insecurity -- especially in vulnerable regions such as the Sahel , the Horn of Africa @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ America and South Asia . UN-backed assessments now consistently identify conflict and insecurity , economic shocks and climate-related extremes as the key converging drivers of acute food insecurity and malnutrition . <h> NEVER AGREE <p> Critics will say the oil industry will never agree to a 75-cent contribution from every US$100 barrel . That may be true if voluntary goodwill is the expectation . But governments can act collectively . Both oil-producing and oil-consuming nations could adopt this solidarity measure at the point of extraction or import -- much as France , Brazil and Norway did when they introduced a modest levy on airline tickets to fund UNITAID 's lifesaving programmes . That mechanism has functioned successfully for nearly two decades , and is now a template for new global solidarity levies . <p> Unlike military spending , which has risen for six consecutive years and reached a record US$2.72 trillion in 2024 , according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute , this humanitarian contribution would be modest , transparent and morally compelling . It would also allow the energy sector -- often criticised for its environmental record and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ great humanitarian achievements of our century . The reputational return for governments and companies would far outweigh the cost . <p> For energy-exporting nations , such a measure could be a diplomatic asset , demonstrating global leadership and compassion at a time when trust is in short supply . For importing nations , it could be an act of solidarity toward a world fracturing under the strain of inequality . And , for multilateral institutions , it would show that cooperation can still cut through an era of fracture and mistrust . <p> This proposal recognises that hunger is not a failure of food production but of political will . International reports show how conflict , climate extremes and economic shocks drive food crises -- from Gaza , Sudan and Ukraine to the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo , Haiti , and climate-vulnerable regions in the Caribbean , Central America , sub-Saharan Africa and the Pacific . These crises persist not because the world lacks means , but because those with power choose inaction . <p> A contribution of US$0.75 per barrel -- far less than the cost of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ child goes to bed hungry , is not charity . It is justice -- long overdue , and well within reach . <p> Sir Ronald Sanders is the ambassador of Antigua and Barbuda to the United States and the OAS . Massive balance-sheet destruction is often accompanied by smaller , but persistent , GDP declines over time . <h> HISTORICAL PATTERN <p> Melissa could well fit this historical pattern . A 13 per cent GDP contraction in one quarter is likely to translate to roughly a three to four per cent annual output loss if concentrated in that period . That is entirely consistent with direct damage of 44 per cent of GDP and total losses likely exceeding national output . <p> This matters because it sets the context for the conversation Jamaica must now have with itself and with the world . Recovery on the scale that Jamaica now needs can not be financed by domestic taxation or by ordinary borrowing without risking debt distress . Pretending otherwise would be economically dishonest and socially dangerous . Indeed , it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ committed to lend to the light and power company , Jamaica Public Service ( JPS ) , for post-Melissa repairs , represents the total amount flowing from the payout of the Government 's catastrophe bond for the hurricane . That process needs to start soon . And with urgency . Minister Williams , therefore , is being looked to for the details . <p> Among the specifics Jamaicans expect to hear from Minister Williams are her initiatives for aggressively pursuing concessional multilateral loans , grant-based climate and disaster financing ; debt-for-climate funding ; and debt-for-resilience swaps . Jamaica should also be looking at expanding catastrophe insurance coverage , as well as other innovative climate finance instruments . <p> It is not unreasonable to expect international help . Jamaica is paying today for climate patterns driven largely by the industrial history of richer nations . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ old development model . But that is not a cause for national despair . <p> Recovery and reconstruction , properly managed , can lift growth , improve productivity , and modernise the economy . However , managed poorly , it can lock Jamaica into debt and disappointment for a generation .
